Situation1: A family member has a significant event they want to share with everyone.
Situation2: They see a swimmer struggling near the middle of the pool and need to stay vigilant to respond quickly.
Story:
I sat on the edge of the pool, whistle around my neck, eyes scanning the water. My daughter called out, her voice bright with excitement, “Dad, come over! Jamie has something to tell everyone!” I glanced over to where my grandson stood, grinning, clearly eager to share his big news. My heart ached to be there, to see his face light up as he told his story, to be the grandparent he remembered as always present.

But my training as a lifeguard kept my gaze fixed on the shimmering blue. Out of the corner of my eye, I noticed a young swimmer in the middle of the pool, their strokes growing uneven, head bobbing just a little too low. The expectation pressed on me: I had to be vigilant, ready to act in an instant. My family’s laughter and anticipation tugged at me from one side, while the silent, urgent responsibility of every swimmer’s safety pulled from the other. My hands tightened on the rescue tube. I felt split in two, torn between the warmth of family and the cold edge of duty, not knowing which call I would answer first.
